https://www.crash.net/f1/news/1101381/1/.text: Russell in Spa © XPB Images Prefer Crash.Net on Google See our stories more often Add George Russell conceded his lack of pace at the Belgian Grand Prix is "infuriating", as the Mercedes driver is "powerless" to stop time bleeding away on the long flat-out sections at the Belgian Grand Prix. Russell has been off the pace compared to Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli on a number of occasions this season, with team boss Toto Wolff instructing the Briton to "just drive" during qualifying for the Austrian Grand Prix. While Russell took pole on that day, the situation was not repeated at Spa-Francorchamps, as he fell half a second shy of his pole-winning team-mate, with almost all of this time being lost on full throttle. “It could be worse, could of been much better," assessed Russell. Russell in Spa © XPB Images Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT "Yesterday, I was losing eight-tenths in the straights; today, I'm losing four-tenths. It's a step in the right direction, but we saw this from Silverstone. We thought we’d found the problem. We thought it was simply the brakes. It wasn't the brakes. Then we thought it was my driving style with the throttle, and I convinced myself that it was something in me with the driving style. “Now, we're very confident it's not the driving style, and that there's a serious issue at play here. The team are working so hard to resolve it. But every lap I do, when I see I'm down anywhere from two-tenths to six-tenths in the straights, it's pretty infuriating.” Read Also Toto Wolff caveats McLaren's Hungary victory after Mercedes' performance dip Ferrari needs to back Hamilton if it wants to end F1 title drought Despite this, Russell maintained that he was "very happy" with his effort and believes that, were it not for the problems in a straight line, he "would have been fighting for the front row". He added: "My whole focus across the last 36 hours has been on straight-line speed. It hasn't been focused on the setup, the tyres, or anything because we're all trying to solve what is going on. “Even on my last lap, for some reason, I lost another tenth and a half to myself just on the straight. And you're watching your lap on your steering wheel just losing speed when you're full straight, when you're full gas on the straight. You feel powerless. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Russell at Spa © XPB Images “So we don't know what's going on. I don't think it's the power unit, to be honest, but there's something slowing us down in the straights. And as I said, the team are really, really on it now to try and solve it.” Asked if he had considered pushing harder in the corners to compensate for the deficit, Russell said: “It's tempting, but my engineer's done a really good job of highlighting where I'm losing, and when I cross the line, you see a half a second down, it feels pretty rubbish. “But when you realise more than 75 percent of that's coming from the power unit, you feel a bit better. As I said, I was pleased with my lap. When I look at the corners, there were a lot of corners where I was faster. There were definitely corners I need to improve, but the corners look like a normal fight you'd have for a pole. The straights are not. "I don't know what the solution is, but I’m praying that, ahead of Budapest week, we find it.” Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Don't miss the latest F1 talking points. https://redditchstandard.co.uk/news/redd.text: Redditch charity gets cash boost to help Eastern European women in the town Ashleigh Osborne 6 th Aug, 2026 Updated: 7 th Aug, 2026 0 THE BRAINCHILD of one Redditch-based Polish woman is about to reap dividends for many more Eastern European women across the county with the award of a National Lottery grant for £9,800. Monika Lenard established her company, Love Growth Network, in 2025 with the express aim of supporting fellow eastern European women who – for all sorts of reasons – were struggling in this country. Monika said she was delighted the National Lottery had recognised the importance of this work with a grant to allow her company to develop and grow. She said: “Over the last 12 to 18 months more and more women, sadly, have been coming to me to tell me about their worries over loneliness, loss of confidence and the ensuing stress this can bring on. “When you are in a strange country and cut off from all your family ties and support then these feelings and worries often seem to multiply. “This grant will allow us to run bi-lingual support sessions for women in a safe space. “The sessions will slowly rebuild the confidence and self-esteem of the women helping to reduce their stress and isolation. “We will call in specialist services when required to offer further help and we will look to help the women reduce their reliance on existing NHS services and resources. “Most importantly though the sessions will be both trauma-informed and bilingual in English, Slovakian, Ukrainian and Polish.” The award of this grant is yet another success for Worcestershire’s Community Boost, the organisation that has generated over £2.4million in grant funding for community organisations. Keith Slater from Worcestershire’s Community Boost worked with Monika on this grant application and is delighted with the award. He said: “We cannot continue to allow groups of vulnerable people to remain almost hidden away and hope that somehow their problems just disappear. “What Monika is offering here is such an important step in helping some quite vulnerable women to recover their self-esteem and improve their general health and well-being.” Visit lovegrowthnetworkcic.org.uk for more information. eastern European women Love Growth Network National Lottery Redditch-based Polish woman Worcestershire’s Community Boost Book an advertisement Submit Your News Stories, Photos & Videos Book an advertisement Popular News 2 weeks ago 0 Chris Helme shows Redditch some love from the 90s at fundraising gig 2 weeks ago 0 IN PICTURES – Thousands flock to Evesham for medieval battle spectacular 2 weeks ago 0 Bike marking event in Redditch helping to combat crime 1 day ago 0 PM Pledges £442m to Get Rough Sleepers Off Streets by Christmas – NATIONAL NEWS 6 days ago 0 Redditch child rapist jailed for 27 years Book an advertisement

Å taudÄ Deep in the forests of central Lithuania, along the banks of the Lietava River, stands an ornate wooden church that seems almost out of place in the wilderness. There are no houses around it. No permanent residents. The road leading to the site winds through remote forest and is difficult to navigate. Yet the church remains â carefully maintained, its carved wooden details preserved, its cemetery tended. This is Perelozai, a former village of Pomor Old Believers whose community disappeared during the second half of the 20th century. Today, the church and cemetery are the only visible reminders of a settlement that once was home to hundreds of people. Perelozai | A. Å taudÄ The Lietava River itself has an unusual place in Lithuanian history. Some historians have suggested that the name Lithuania may have originated from the river's name, although the etymology remains debated. For centuries, Perelozai was part of a much larger story: the migration of Russian Old Believers to the lands of the former Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, where they sought refuge from religious persecution. A religious split The history of Old Believers in Lithuania dates to 1679, when some of those fleeing persecution settled in what is now Lithuania. Their flight followed a major religious rupture in 17th-century Russia. Patriarch Nikon, backed by Tsar Alexei Mikhailovich, introduced reforms intended to bring Russian Orthodox religious practices closer to those of the Greek Orthodox Church. Patriarch Nikon and Tsar Alexis ordering the revision of liturgy. A painting by Aleksey Kivshenko | Wikipedia Some of the changes may appear minor today. Worshippers were instructed to make the sign of the cross with three fingers rather than two. The singing of âAlleluiaâ changed from two repetitions to three. Processions around churches were to move in the opposite direction, the number of bows during prayers was reduced, and changes were made to chanting, the shape of the cross and the spelling of Jesusâ name in icons and religious texts. For many believers and priests, however, these were not minor changes. They viewed them as a betrayal of the faith and refused to abandon established traditions. The resulting split in the Russian Orthodox Church became permanent. Perelozai cemetery | A. Å taudÄ The church authorities condemned the old rituals and books as erroneous and heretical at the 1666-67 Moscow Church Council, and those who rejected the reforms were excommunicated. The anathema was formally lifted only in 1971. The Old Believers who resisted the reforms faced persecution, torture and executions. Under Peter the Great, economic pressure was added to religious repression. Old Believers could be subjected to double taxation and a separate beard tax. Many fled west. Refuge in the forests Old Believers began settling in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in the second half of the 17th century, often choosing remote, heavily forested areas far from major roads. Their arrival coincided with a period when large parts of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania had been devastated by wars and plague epidemics. Local landowners were willing to accept newcomers who were regarded as hardworking, sober and skilled in different trades. Perelozai old believers church | Shutterstock The settlers were given land and various concessions. Many learned Polish and Lithuanian and became established members of their communities. By 1772, an estimated 180,000 Old Believers lived in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. In Lithuania, large concentrations developed around Zarasai, with significant communities also in the areas of RokiÅ¡kis, Jonava, KupiÅ¡kis, BirÅ¾ai and Seinai. Their villages were often tucked away in forests. Over generations, Lithuanian Old Believers preserved distinctive traditions, including their style of religious singing, icon painting and bronze casting. Their religious books were published and copied, while elements of older Russian vocabulary survived in their language. Perelozai emerges Old Believers arrived in Perelozai during a second wave of migration in the second half of the 18th century, during the reign of Catherine the Great. Her policies toward Old Believers fluctuated, with periods of renewed repression followed by greater tolerance. The Perelozai settlement is believed to have been established near the end of the 18th century, when its first church was also built. By the middle of the 19th century, about 150 Old Believers lived in the village. Perelozai | A. Å taudÄ Around 1870, lightning struck the church and its roof burned down. The impoverished priestless community could not afford to rebuild it, and worshippers used a temporary prayer house for years. The Russian authorities continued to restrict Old Believers, particularly during the reign of Tsar Nicholas I. They sought to pressure or persuade them to join the official Orthodox Church and restricted the construction and repair of Old Believer churches. After the 1905 Russian Revolution, those restrictions were eased. Nicholas II was forced to grant Old Believers greater civil rights, including the right to build and repair houses of worship. A new church was built in Perelozai on the stone foundations of the earlier one. Its construction was financed by wealthy Vilnius Old Believers, including members of the Pimonov family, a prominent family of real estate magnates. Professional craftsmen were hired and building materials purchased. The community also acquired religious items, icons made according to the old canon, religious books and silver liturgical vessels. Perelozai cemetery | A. Å taudÄ The church was repaired and reinforced during the interwar period, giving it essentially the appearance it retains today. During World War Two, German forces took away both of its bells. A village that disappeared Perelozai was once more than a religious settlement. A school and community centre operated there in the 19th century. At the beginning of the 20th century, about 500 believers belonged to the parish. A ferry operated across the nearby Neris River from the mid-19th century until the postwar period. With few bridges in the area and forests and wetlands making travel difficult, the crossing was important to local residents and loggers. It was also used by smugglers and postwar partisans. Women from Perelozai were known for baking bread and pastries. During religious celebrations, they prepared poppy-seed-covered rings of sweet bread and braided loaves. Perelozai cemetery | A. Å taudÄ After World War Two, the parish grew to about 850 people. Then the village began to fade. Collectivisation disrupted the traditional rural way of life, while younger residents increasingly moved to towns. As the population dwindled, the religious community was officially deregistered in 1984 as having âdisintegratedâ. By 2011, there were no residents left. Perelozai cemetery | A. Å taudÄ Today, there are no houses in Perelozai. Only the church and cemetery remain. The cemetery contains graves dating back to the late 18th century. The church, with its two towers and elaborate wooden carvings, has been restored and is maintained by members of the Old Believer community. Descendants of Perelozaiâs former residents and their relatives still return for religious holidays and community workdays, when they clean the cemetery, maintain the grounds and care for the church. The Christa Pike horror show continues after Tennessee botched her execution for a horrific murder she committed in 1995. She was sentenced to death after her conviction, at age 20, one of the youngest women to receive a death sentence. Her childhood had been harrowing, with alcoholic parents and sexual abuse from a young age and into her teens. After over twenty years in prison, Tennessee went forward with her execution, but subjected her to torture instead, as two attempts to inject her with the deadly dose of pentobarbital, with at least seven needles put into her arm, failed to kill her. It was over an hour before she was transferred to the hospital. On Monday, she was unconscious and on a ventilator. Hospital officials believed she was brain-dead and would need to be taken off life support. On Tuesday, she regained consciousness. Wednesday, though very weak and cognitively confused, she was awake enough to recognize that she was shackled to a bed. Her first words were “Where am I, and who are you?” Memories of her execution attempt have been coming back gradually. The horror has reignited the debate over capital punishment. Some states are continuing to move forward with their executions, but in California, Gov. Gavin Newsom is considering sparing the lives of all 563 prisoners on Death Row in California. At the other end of the spectrum from state-sponsored execution, I’d like to highlight this news story because this very week a book came out about this complicated global debate over assisted dying: Fight to the Death: The Human Stories Shaping America’s MAID Debate , by Paul Brand, one of this week’s 20% off picks at The Literate Lizard. (The acronym MAID stands for Medical Assistance or Medical Aid in Dying.)
